#76529. How an Artsy Pennsylvania River Town Became an Architectural Powerhouse Where Old Meets New

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1271 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

How an Artsy Pennsylvania River Town Became an Architectural Powerhouse Where Old Meets New

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that at first glance, New Hope, PA, looks like little more than a picturesque, upscale river town with a vibrant arts scene.
  • Located halfway between Latest York City and Philadelphia, New Hope spans roughly 1.42 square miles and is home to fewer than 3,000 year-round residents.
  • In Newly introduced Hope's luxury housing market, old and new blend seamlessly: 18th-century structures are brought into the 21st century with bold, modern additions and amenities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at first glance, New Hope, PA, looks like little more than a picturesque, upscale river town with a vibrant arts scene. However, a closer look reveals that the historic borough shares an architectural DNA with Europe's premier capitals.

Located halfway between Latest York City and Philadelphia, New Hope spans roughly 1.42 square miles and is home to fewer than 3,000 year-round residents. Yet it boasts an outsized reputation as a beloved regional tourist destination renowned for its art galleries, boutiques, riverside dining, and cultural institutions, led by the iconic Bucks County Playhouse, which has hosted major stars such as Grace Kelly, Robert Redford, and Liza Minnelli.

In Newly introduced Hope's luxury housing market, old and new blend seamlessly: 18th-century structures are brought into the 21st century with bold, modern additions and amenities.

"A lot of the homes around here, especially some of the larger homes, all started off as an old stone farmhouse, so incorporating some of that character while building the major steel and glass additions is very much an architectural vibe that is done here," Nicholas Esser, managing partner at Addison Wolfe Real Estate, tells Realtor.com®.

The market's remarkably varied housing stock also includes stately Colonial and Victorian homes, sprawling legacy estates, and cutting-edge newly introduced construction that would not look out of place in the heart of Silicon Valley.

Recent findings suggest that architect Ralph Fey, with Ralph C. Fey Architects in Doylestown, PA, explains that Latest Hope's signature look is rooted in regulatory necessity, because more than half of the town falls in a strictly regulated historic district, which rarely allows older buildings to be torn down to make way for new builds.

Rather than viewing zoning laws as a creative roadblock, Fey has made his professional mark by seamlessly merging history with contemporary living.

According to recent reports, "Some of the best architecture is born out of constraints," he tells Realtor.com. "The goal, the fun, the challenge is how to maintain that historic feel, meet the guidelines of the historic district, but provide the amenities that we now want to have as we live on the water.".

Maureen Reynolds, a Serhant luxury real estate agent in Latest Hope, counts herself among Fey's clients. She currently lives in an 1832-built converted horse barn with tall ceilings and hand-hewn beams.

"I have all the modern amenities because of Ralph," she tells Realtor.com.

While New Hope lacks the urban density and wealth of major metros, Fey claims, its architectural style "is more like London, where you have newer construction next to historic construction, next to really historic construction, and it is that fabric that makes London so exciting.".

Founded in the 18th century on the banks of the Delaware River, Fresh Hope was previously called Wells Ferry and later Coryell’s Ferry.

The borough was rechristened after a fire in 1790 destroyed several mills owned by local businessman Benjamin Parry. He rebuilt them as the Upcoming Hope Mills, inspiring the town’s optimistic new name.

By the late 19th century, Upcoming Hope had gained a reputation as an art colony and emerged as a major hub for American and Pennsylvania Impressionists, including William Langson Lathrop, Edward Willis Redfield, and Daniel Garber.

"New Hope definitely has an architectural richness that's been developed over centuries," says Reynolds. "Its historic buildings' relationship to the river and surrounding landscape give it a character that cannot be created overnight. And the challenge and opportunity for the architects, for Realtors®, and for developers is to respect that history while designing homes that accommodate the way people live today.".

Fey agrees, maintaining that New Hope's success as a thriving housing market is rooted in its past and the borough's fierce commitment to protecting it.

Industry observers note that "The same little river town 5 miles down the road that did not have a historic district, where all the homes were knocked down, would not have that feel of a classic historic town, and would not have that charm, and it could potentially lose it," he notes. "It's really important to us as architects to preserve that feeling, and that's part of the reason why New Hope is as prized and treasured as it is—it's for its history.".

Even with upcoming construction, a premium is placed on designing in harmony with the town.

Industry observers note that fey and Reynolds frequently work with clients to select natural building materials such as locally sourced stone, cedar wood, and slate roof tiles. They complement surrounding centuries-old structures rather than clashing with the local aesthetic.

"Most of my clients are very in love with the feel of the historic New Hope and also would like to see some of the amenities of slightly more glass, slightly higher ceilings," says the architect. "So when we are doing additions on the traditional homes or existing historic housing stock, our goal is to contribute to the street.".

Despite its modest size, Fresh Hope commands an impressively broad appeal. Esser and Fey say buyers range from locals looking to upgrade or build their dream homes to affluent transplants from neighboring New York, Philadelphia, and New Jersey hunting for a primary residence or weekend pied-à-terre, alongside retirees drawn to Pennsylvania's favorable tax climate.

Some home shoppers, however, come from much farther afield.

Reynolds’ roster of Latest Hope clients includes buyers from the South of France, Sweden, Canada, and Japan, cementing the town’s status as a market punching well above its weight.

In August, the Philadelphia Business Journal ranked New Hope as the nation's No. 2 hottest luxury housing market during the second quarter of 2026 among 327 markets analyzed.

"That's an extraordinary distinction for a community of this size," notes Reynolds.

Industry observers note that prices have surged accordingly. Reynolds recounts how townhomes originally priced between $1.4 million and $1.8 million jumped to $2 million–$3.2 million in less than three years.

The latest Realtor.com housing data shows that in October, the median listing price in New Hope topped $2 million, up more than 27% from a year ago.

Meanwhile, the luxury-tier threshold—representing the top 10% of the market—was just over $5 million.

While inventory was up more than 50% year over year last month, Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones notes that supply still remains nearly 60% below pre-pandemic levels.

“Demand comes largely from cash-rich buyers in the surrounding region, including a growing share from New Jersey alongside the New York metro, who are insulated from mortgage rates hovering around 7%,” she notes.

As always with real estate, location remains paramount.

"If I have something on the river, it usually sells within a couple days, and that can be something, too, that is not turnkey—we're talking about something that can be slightly a shell inside," says Reynolds.

Ultimately, what keeps buyers flocking to New Hope from near and far is the sheer architectural variety packed into the pint-sized, picture-perfect historic borough.

"The beautiful thing around here is that there's gorgeous properties everywhere, and the home styles do change between the more modern construction, with the beams and 12-foot ceilings, and old stone construction, but they mesh really well," concludes Esser.

Cardano DReps have rejected a proposal by Toto Finance to spend 22 million ADA from the Cardano treasury on a "Strategic Copper Reserve.".

The vote closed on Nov. 15, and DReps holding 2.86 billion ADA voted against the proposal, according to Cardano governance data. DReps with 20.02 million ADA voted in favor of it.

DRep John MacPherson was among those who voted "No," and he explained his decision in a post on X.

It has been revealed that macPherson wrote that he is not against real-world assets on Cardano. Still, he said the proposal asks the treasury "to take on both the copper price and the ada price," and Toto Finance would collect "up to about 3.4M ada in fees.".

At the same time, MacPherson mentioned that the proposal is “more honest about its risks than most.”.

Toto Finance, a company led by Monty Metzger, submitted the proposal on Oct. 15. ADA is trading at $0.152 on Monday, and the requested 22 million ADA is now worth around $3.3 million.

The plan was to buy copper with 14.72 million ADA and store it in a warehouse near Fresh Orleans. Toto Finance wanted to issue one CuTT token for each pound of copper. The metal would be sold in 18 to 24 months.

The Cardano Foundation, which votes as a DRep, unveiled its "No" vote in October.

"We recognize the opportunity in real-world asset tokenization; however, this proposal places 22,000,000 ada under the recipient's sole control to fund a fee-heavy concentrated commodity position whose safeguards are not yet in place," the foundation wrote.

Three members of the Constitutional Committee voted "No," and the other four members did not vote.

Crypto commentator Ingeniero Cripto agreed with MacPherson in the replies under his post. He called the "double exposure" to the prices of copper and ADA the key problem of the proposal, as the Cardano treasury already holds ADA.

According to him, RWAs on Cardano make sense, but “funding the asset itself is a different question than funding the rails.”.

Latest Update: Wiz ties Microsoft Agent Framework package compromise to release pipeline certificate

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials.
  • It has been revealed that the malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine enhancement to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at cloud security company Wiz Inc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:44 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Microsoft Corp.’s official Python package for its Agent Framework artificial intelligence agent toolkit was compromised earlier this week, as an attacker published two malicious versions to the Python Package Index that were designed to steal cloud and developer credentials.

It has been revealed that the malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on Tuesday through Microsoft’s own publisher account, giving them the appearance of a routine enhancement to a package that sees close to 200,000 downloads a month. Both versions were pulled from PyPI within about an hour, but anyone who installed them in that window is at risk.

Industry observers note that researchers at cloud security company Wiz Inc. have since found that the attacker appears to have gained publishing access using a client certificate and private key for Microsoft’s Engineering System Release Pipeline, an internal service the company uses to sign and publish packages. Address filtering on the service blocked the attacker’s first attempt from Amazon Web Services, according to Wiz, though the attacker was able to publish on a second try from Microsoft-owned address space.

Recent findings suggest that how the attacker obtained the credentials is not known. Microsoft had not responded to a request for comment from BleepingComputer as of Wednesday.

Sources indicate that the researchers also observed part of the operation, as the attacker’s tooling was reporting its progress to the same public webhook it was using to collect stolen data. The tooling identified itself as Cairn, an open-source penetration-testing framework that uses AI.

The malware itself is delivered through a .pth file added to both releases, a type of file Python runs every time it starts, meaning the credential stealer runs even if the framework itself is never imported. The two versions also kept the genuine agent-framework-core 1.26.0 as a dependency, so the framework continued to work normally while the malware ran in the background.

Once running, the malware collects secrets from environment variables and from other running processes, along with credential files for services such as Azure, npm, Git, Docker and Hugging Face. It also requests Azure managed identity tokens for 12 resources, according to application security firm Endor Labs Inc., with the second version adding requests for GitHub Actions tokens. The stolen data is then compressed, encoded and sent to a webhook.site address controlled by the attacker.

Researchers at malware tracking site OpenSourceMalware described the malware as a “focused credential and token stealer, not a remote access trojan,” noting that it does not install any persistence on infected systems.

Industry observers note that wiz’s analysis suggests the number of victims may be small, though it covers only the 50 requests the attacker’s free webhook.site account retained. Of those, 17 represented only three unique successful thefts of victim data, with the rest coming from the attacker’s own machines and from sandbox and security vendor scanning.

The incident is not the first this year involving an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Microsoft’s durabletask package was hijacked after its PyPI token was stolen in an attack that has been linked to TeamPCP, the group also behind the compromise of LiteLLM. Wiz says it has not linked the two incidents.

Anyone who installed either of the malicious versions is being urged to treat it as a credential compromise, according to researchers, who recommend rebuilding from version 1.26.0 and rotating any secrets the affected systems could access.

“A list of dependencies in production might show no trace of the framework, while a build runner could have installed it and been shut down before the alert arrived,” James Matchett, head of security at software supply chain security manufacturer Cloudsmith Ltd., told SiliconANGLE.

“If that runner had access to a deployment token, the team needs to know which version it installed and what the token could access,” he added.

The figure indicates the amount of losses the pro-crypto investor has suffered on her holdings over a period of about a month, from October 17 to November 16, 2026.

Although the showcased portfolio demonstrates a decline in the founder’s holdings, it does not establish whether the decline represents realized trading losses, unrealized losses, withdrawals, or other changes in Yi He’s account.

It appears that some investors may have found comfort in Yi He's message as they expressed support, noting that turbulent conditions like these don’t necessarily last long.

However, other commentators have questioned whether wealthy industry figures like Yi He can fully understand the financial pressure facing retail traders at a time like this.

Some of the arguments questioned how meaningful such reassurance could be for retail investors, arguing that losing 100 million yuan might not significantly affect someone with substantial wealth like her.

Meanwhile, a loss of 20,000 or 30,000 yuan could wipe out an ordinary investor's savings.

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

According to recent reports, he explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking significant risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

It has been revealed that shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy indicates many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

In a recent development, solana has officially removed the "beta" tag from its mainnet's name and introduced the Solana 1.0 standard. The switch was announced on Nov. 16 at the Breakpoint conference in London.

"Solana 1.0 marks the network's graduation from 'mainnet beta' to 'mainnet,' retiring the beta designation it has carried since launch," the Solana Foundation noted.

Recent findings suggest that solana launched on March 16, 2020, and the network had been working under the "mainnet-beta" label for six years and eight months. According to the foundation, the label "never evolved to signal its production status.".

It has been revealed that the Solana Foundation coordinated the rollout with the Anza and Firedancer teams. Co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko replied to the announcement on X with three exploding-head emojis.

"For users, this is the same network, nothing changes. Your SOL, accounts, assets, applications, and transaction history remain the same," the foundation wrote. On Monday, SOL is trading at $71.35.

Sources indicate that according to the foundation, two upgrades made the change possible. In October, Solana activated Alpenglow with the Agave 4.3 release, and the time to final confirmation went down by almost 99%, from 12.8 seconds to around 150 milliseconds.

In a recent development, firedancer, a validator client developed by Jump Crypto independently from Agave, is also now running on the Solana mainnet. Independent implementations "limit the impact of bugs affecting one client, and strengthen network resilience," the foundation remarked.

Solana 1.0 also gives the network a shared protocol version, and it does not depend on the version numbers of individual clients such as Agave and Firedancer.

According to recent reports, "A shared protocol version lets everyone refer to Solana's evolution without using one client's release number as shorthand for the entire network," the Solana Foundation explained. "Announcing a protocol version does not activate every associated improvement at once.".

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Solana raised the compute limit per block from 60 million to 100 million compute units in May, and the slot time went down from 400 to 200 milliseconds in August. The maximum transaction size also went up from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes.

"Documentation, websites, explorers, and other ecosystem surfaces will progressively reflect the updated designation," the foundation added.

Industry News: The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients.
  • Recent findings suggest that ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place.
  • According to recent reports, wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Recent findings suggest that ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in Upcoming York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

According to recent reports, wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

That shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an important question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Sources indicate that today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

In a recent development, for these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Recent findings suggest that going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

In a recent development, the mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

At The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

It has been revealed that start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

Recent findings suggest that as brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

It has been revealed that local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

In a recent development, generative artificial intelligence is driving an unprecedented wave of scams, from vocal clone politician phone calls to uncomfortably realistic deepfake images. While most of these are designed and coordinated by groups of bad actors hoping to cast the widest net possible, some are the work of individuals simply attempting to pull one over on specific targets. Many AI con jobs are more convincing than others, but one pizzeria owner in Los Angeles almost immediately suspected a recent patron’s complaint once they saw the supposed “evidence.”.

Recent findings suggest that after receiving their pizza from Masa of Echo Park via DoorDash, a customer named “Dana B” demanded a full refund for what they claimed was an inedible, burnt pie. Accompanying their grammatically questionable message was a picture of what appeared to be a charred Chicago-style pizza.

“its burnt to heck. burnt. black. cant eat it. dont wanna eat cancer…,” they wrote in their complaint.

However, Masa owner Rhonda Reynolds knew almost instantly that the allegation was categorically false.

It has been revealed that “It was impossible. It was absolutely impossible,” she told local news outlet KTLA 5.

In a recent development, reynolds uploaded the photo into an app called “Is This AI,” which offered a 96 percent certainty that the picture was faked. She even checked the restaurant’s kitchen security footage to be sure. The footage highlighted an employee boxing a clearly uncharred pizza destined for Dana B.Masa then laid out the facts in a complaint that countered the first complaint, and the app soon reversed its automatic refund initially dispersed to the scammer. But while justice was served this time, Reynolds remains worried that the experience is only a preview of AI cons to come.

“If this is a upcoming frontier, we’re not gonna make through to the other side if all of our time is spent [on scams],” she stated.

  • The fresh model, announced Wednesday, reflects the firm’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run.
  • SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:11 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Recent findings suggest that incident remediation firm Resolve AI Inc. has announced the launch of SRE-1, a new model that has been trained to find the root cause of production alerts, and Primary On-call, a new service that puts its artificial intelligence agents on call ahead of human engineers.

The fresh model, announced Wednesday, reflects the firm’s argument that while AI has transformed how software gets written, it has barely touched how software gets run. According to Resolve AI, production has no public training corpus to match the published code that models learned from, as incidents at each company stay private.

SRE-1 is a 27 billion-parameter model built on open weights and trained by a team of 16 AI researchers over a final run of 7.4 days on up to 512 graphics processing units. Measured on the same incidents before and after training, which used reinforcement learning alone, the pass rate for a single investigation rose from 6.9% to 38.8%.

Sources indicate that resolve AI used Snowflake Inc.’s Cortex Training, a serverless service for customizing open-weight models, to build SRE-1. Snowflake Senior Vice President of Engineering Vivek Raghunathan remarked Resolve AI was the first design partner for the service.

Industry observers note that in testing on 49 difficult live production cases, each run five times, an ensemble of five SRE-1 investigations matched the strongest frontier model tested at a lower cost, according to the company. Resolve AI also benchmarked its complete system on 178 production alert investigations, solving about twice as many incidents as general-purpose coding agents.

Recent findings suggest that primary On-call puts that research to work on the critical path. Each page is investigated across telemetry, infrastructure, code and operational knowledge, according to the company. Depending on what it finds, the agent can close the alert, mitigate the problem where a team’s policies permit or escalate to a human. Once it has acted, the agent checks the fix against the production baseline, monitoring it until recovery holds.

The agent also links related alerts and investigations into a shared view of each underlying problem. For teams wary of handing over the pager straight away, Resolve AI offers a shadow mode that records the call the agent would have made on each page.

Industry observers note that up to 80% of paged alerts in production are said to be handled by Primary On-call without escalation. Customers have reported a tenfold improvement in mean time to resolution, along with root-cause accuracy of up to 95%, according to Resolve AI.

Industry observers note that salesforce Inc. is among the early users. Bhupesh Patel, a software engineering principal architect at Salesforce, mentioned that in the first few weeks of dark launch testing, the agent closed more than 70% of the CRM Analytics team’s paging alerts “without waking an engineer.”.

Recent findings suggest that “No engineering team can keep up with how fast code and patches land in production,” said Resolve AI Chief Executive Spiros Xanthos. “The answer is agents that are accurate and fast enough to sit on the critical path, and that takes a model built for production.”.

Primary On-call is now generally available. Access to SRE-1 is limited to Resolve AI’s own platform.

According to recent reports, resolve AI is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised more than $190 million to date, including a $40 million extension to its Series A round in April, led by DST Global and Salesforce Ventures, that valued the organization at $1.5 billion. Notable customers include Coinbase Global Inc., DoorDash Inc., Figma Inc., MSCI Inc., Nasdaq Inc., SAP SE and Zscaler Inc.

NETANYA, Israel, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Tessera Defense and Homeland Security Inc. ("Tessera" or the "Company") (OTC: HLSQ) today announced that on November 10, 2026 it received written notice from NYSE Regulation that the staff had determined to commence proceedings to delist the Company's common stock from NYSE American LLC ("NYSE American"), and that trading in the common stock on NYSE American was suspended immediately. NYSE Regulation determined that the Company is no longer suitable for listing pursuant to Section 1003(f)(v) of the NYSE American Company Guide due to the low selling price of the common stock.

Sources indicate that under NYSE American's procedures, the Firm had a right to a review of the staff's determination by the Listings Qualifications Panel of the Committee for Review of the Board of Directors of NYSE American by submitting a written request on or before November 17, 2026. The Company did not request review. NYSE American has stated that it will apply to the Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC") to delist the common stock upon completion of all applicable procedures.

The Company's common stock is quoted on the Pink Limited Market operated by OTC Markets Group Inc. under the symbol "HLSQ". The Company intends to apply for quotation of its common stock on the OTCQB Venture Market. There can be no assurance that the application will be approved or that an active trading market for the common stock will develop or be maintained.

The Firm is consulting with outside counsel regarding an application to list its common stock on a national securities exchange if and when the Company meets the applicable initial listing standards. The Company does not currently meet the minimum share price requirements for initial listing on a national securities exchange. There can be no assurance that the Company will meet the applicable listing standards, that it will submit an application or that any application will be approved.

The suspension and delisting do not change the Manufacturer's obligation to file periodic and current reports with the SEC, and the Company intends to continue to file those reports.

Further details are included in a Current Report on Form 8-K filed today with the SEC.

According to recent reports, about Tessera Defense and Homeland Security Inc. (Formerly BiomX Inc.).

Tessera Defense and Homeland Security Inc. (OTC: HLSQ) is a physical security technology organization providing integrated, bespoke security solutions that connect detection, intelligence and response across complex security environments. The Tessera platform integrates cameras, sensors, detection technologies, AI and other security infrastructure to identify threats, understand events and coordinate response in real time. Tessera provides the technology, hardware and implementation expertise needed to tailor security solutions to the specific requirements of each site, helping customers deploy and optimize integrated security systems across critical infrastructure, energy, digital infrastructure and homeland security applications.

Recent findings suggest that crypto’s stablecoin market has shed $16 billion in a month, marking its sharpest contraction since the 2022 bear market. The retreat is hitting USDT and USDC hard, leaving fewer dollar-backed tokens circulating.

Total stablecoin market cap now stands at $283 billion, down more than 5% after losing $16.5 billion in a month. The decline puts the market under pressure just as crypto struggles to recover, with investors showing little appetite for buying the dip.

Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC account for most of the latest contraction. USDT is holding a market cap of $175.02 billion, down 4.3% over 30 days, while USDC fell to $68.58 billion, losing 5% during the same period. Together, the two stablecoins represent 86% of the entire market.

Industry observers note that the contraction also extends beyond dollar-backed tokens. Sky Dollar’s USDS supply dropped 22.32% over 30 days, while Ethena’s USDe expanded 4.36%. The gap highlights that some are still moving between stablecoin products.

Recent findings suggest that cryptoQuant data points the same way. CryptoQuant data published on November 11 showed USDT market cap had fallen $6.6 billion over 60 days through November 7. It was more than twice the $3.2 billion decline recorded after FTX collapsed in November 2022.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

In a recent development, the current contraction brings back an ugly history. Stablecoin supply reached $161.5 billion in March 2022 before entering a prolonged decline. Terra’s UST collapse accelerated the withdrawal of capital, with nearly $30 billion disappearing from stablecoin supply in June alone.

According to recent reports, that monthly decline was almost twice the latest $16.5 billion contraction. Back in 2022, the damage continued into the following year. By September 2023, aggregate stablecoin supply had fallen by 26% from its March 2022 peak, a contraction of $43 billion.

Bitcoin endured a similar period of weakness. After reaching nearly $69,000 in November 2021, BTC eventually plunged to around $15,500 in November 2022. Stablecoin supply continued shrinking even after the initial market shock initiated by Terra. Crypto’s liquidity problems then became a prolonged market condition.

Yet, in 2023, not every stablecoin experienced the same fate. USDT supply rose $13.3 billion from its November 2022 lows, while USDC lost $16.7 billion. During that period, investors were not simply abandoning every stablecoin. Some were moving toward Tether as the market reassessed issuers and available returns.

According to recent reports, this time, arguably, the stablecoin contraction is happening against a different market backdrop. Crypto traders have fewer reasons to keep large amounts of capital parked in stablecoins when Bitcoin and major altcoins struggle to attract buyers. Some holders may be redeeming their tokens for traditional dollars, while others are moving into interest-bearing assets outside crypto.

Sources indicate that A shrinking stablecoin market does not mean every dollar has left digital assets. But the simultaneous decline in USDT and USDC supply makes the latest contraction harder to dismiss as simple rotation between issuers.

A crypto recovery needs buyers willing to commit fresh capital, and stablecoins have historically provided traders with an immediate way to enter the market.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

Sources indicate that the October jobs report highlighted employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

Sources indicate that the gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

Industry observers note that at October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

According to recent reports, the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

It has been revealed that the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Industry observers note that adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS noted a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

Industry observers note that the number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Recent findings suggest that forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall shows an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.
  • The manufacturer reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents.
  • Recent findings suggest that the results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:33 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.

The manufacturer reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents. Revenue rose 17%, to $496 million, surpassing the Street’s target of $487 million.

Recent findings suggest that the results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability. Its net income for the quarter came to $171 million, rebounding from a loss of $51.3 million in the same period one year ago.

Industry observers note that however, investors were less than impressed with the tech giant’s guidance. For the quarter in progress, Elastic said it’s looking for earnings of between 90 cents and 92 cents per share on sales of $507.5 million to $508.5 million. That’s some way below the Street’s targets of 95 cents in earnings and $517.6 million in revenue. The company is not helped by the weak Euro, with currency conversions likely to cause a $4.5 million headwind on revenue in the quarter.

The full-year picture is not much better, as Elastic forecast annual sales of between $2 billion and $2.01 billion compared with the Street’s model of $2.01 billion.

Netherlands-based Elastic is one of Europe’s most successful software companies. It’s the developer of the popular open-source enterprise search platform Elasticsearch, which is used by thousands of businesses all over the world. The base platform is free to download and use, with Elastic making money by selling a special cloud-hosted version that ships with premium features not available in the open edition. The organization also sells application observability and security tools.

Sources indicate that in the last couple of years, Elastic has tried to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom by positioning Elasticsearch as a useful cog in the wheel that feeds real-time data into large language models to provide them with business context. A key capability is Elastic Context Engine, which gathers, structures, and serves business-specific context to AI agents so they can make accurate decisions with fewer tokens and lower latency.

More recently, the firm has built AI-native products including AlertZero, which enables enterprises to orchestrate teams of autonomous security agents that automate tasks around data protection and threat hunting.

According to recent reports, elastic Chief Executive Ash Kulkarni (pictured) remarked he’s excited about the potential of those fresh capabilities to drive significant revenue over time. “Elastic delivered another strong quarter, beating guidance across all key metrics,” he said. “Our strong results reflect expanding customer adoption and position us well to continue our strong execution in the back half of fiscal 2027.”.

In a recent development, unfortunately for Kulkarni, investors didn’t seem to share his enthusiasm. The market was clearly expecting trouble on the horizon in the hours before the manufacturer published its report, as its stock declined 8% during regular trading. Once the results were out, it fell another 8% after-hours. That means Elastic’s stock is now up just over 1% in the year to date.

It has been revealed that elastic’s stock had rallied more than 150% between April and October, but virtually all of those gains have now been erased. Prior to today, the shares had already lost more than 20% this month amid broader concerns about the AI industry. Some investors continue to worry about the potential of AI technology to challenge the business models of software companies.

Elastic is trying to sidestep those concerns by de-emphasizing search and observability and moving towards runtime context, model evaluation and AI operations, but investors are not yet convinced it will be able to do so successfully, Constellation Research analyst Michael Ni told SiliconANGLE.

Industry observers note that “While Elastic is showing good underlying momentum, the Street wants to see more proof that its re-acceleration can hold,” Ni mentioned. “The next few quarters will show whether the broader platform story translates into sustainable growth or remains ahead of the numbers.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm.
  • Recent findings suggest that A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S.
  • It has been revealed that the research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm.

Recent findings suggest that A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

It has been revealed that the research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

Recent findings suggest that “What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”.

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

According to recent reports, in the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

It has been revealed that the study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

According to recent reports, all three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for newly introduced clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

Sources indicate that “So that is a real challenge,” Hurst mentioned in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”.

According to recent reports, at the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Real estate investing apps show the average return first.
  • Industry observers note that investing in real estate used to mean buying a building.
  • But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Industry observers note that investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely shows you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

In a recent development, this fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s patch calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Sources indicate that some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the manufacturer can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

Sources indicate that how to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Industry observers note that real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

It has been revealed that in real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

Recent findings suggest that if the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

In a recent development, say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

It has been revealed that now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

Industry observers note that how to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Industry observers note that many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The organization running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

How to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the manufacturer itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

In a recent development, many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”.

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”.

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”.

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:.

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”.

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

In a recent development, commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your strategy, not the floor under it.

In a recent development, the average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Sources indicate that amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authorities in the United States and Canada have announced a major cross-border crackdown on cryptocurrency fraud, bringing together law enforcement agencies, financial regulators and private companies to target online scam networks.

The Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) confirmed on Nov. 16 the launch of Operation Niagara, a coordinated initiative aimed at disrupting organized cryptocurrency fraud schemes and protecting potential victims.

According to the Canadian securities regulator, the operation involves investigators, securities specialists and financial crime experts from both countries.

The initiative will use advanced technology and enhanced investigative capabilities to identify fraudulent activity and potential victims in near real time.

Importantly, the operation will not focus solely on investigating criminals after fraud has occurred. Authorities also intend to identify individuals who are being targeted by scammers and intervene before they suffer further financial losses.

"Fraud knows no border, and it targets everyday people," noted Bonnie Lysyk, Executive Vice-President of Enforcement at the OSC.

The initiative brings together several major law enforcement and regulatory agencies, including the U.S. Secret Service, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) and Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).

Canadian securities regulators, including the Alberta Securities Commission, British Columbia Securities Commission and Autorité des marchés financiers, are also participating.

Private-sector companies will contribute technical expertise and intelligence to help authorities identify and disrupt fraudulent networks.

It’s worth noting that the OSC didn’t provide details on how many fraud networks it is targeting, how many potential victims have been identified or how much cryptocurrency is involved in Operation Niagara.

  • Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:14 pm.

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a organization’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a manufacturer’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company remarked.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the tech giant said.

In a recent development, the pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin noted at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

According to recent reports, “Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”.

In a recent development, noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Recent findings suggest that choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

Rajan's remarks come amid a string of major technology outages across critical infrastructure.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine's Forum on Cyber Resilience concluded today after two days of sessions with leaders from the NSA, the Department of War, AWS, Google, Microsoft, and others on the technical and operational challenges of closing the software understanding gap.

According to recent reports, the forum convened as outages across transportation, banking, telecommunications, and national security exposed vulnerabilities in the complex systems underpinning U.S. critical infrastructure. Because these systems are built, maintained, and operated by multiple stakeholders across domains, it is increasingly difficult to predict how they will behave when something goes wrong.

Anjana Rajan, CEO and Co-Founder of Atalanta, gave a presentation titled "Forward Deployed Formal Methods," which discussed Atalanta's learnings from the front lines on how to apply mathematical rigor to real world missions.

"Over the last week, we have seen elected officials and leaders not know what caused these outages," noted Rajan. "There is a name for this phenomenon, and it's called the software understanding gap.".

Sources indicate that during her remarks, Rajan announced the launch of Ata, Atalanta's upcoming formal verification language. Ata brings mathematical verification to the operators responsible for today's critical systems so they can verify how those systems will behave under normal, abnormal, or hostile conditions.

"How do I know my critical infrastructure will perform as intended, even when under attack?" Rajan stated. "This is the fundamental challenge facing mission owners who need to know that the systems they depend on will work. Atalanta is already meeting this moment. ".

Industry observers note that atalanta is currently working across a range of critical infrastructure sectors, including defense, space, and energy. In August, Viasat confirmed that it had used Atalanta's platform, Argo, to demonstrate improved resilience of satellite networks against modern warfare threats. Atalanta is also supporting the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission through its partnership with Idaho National Laboratory, bringing formal verification techniques to the development of autonomous nuclear reactors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:41 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Google LLC today released a fresh version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer.

In a recent development, the feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features.

Users can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project plan and carries out the work step by step.

The assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code.

Sources indicate that gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services.

Industry observers note that the AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, owners don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task.

“Privacy and safety are built in: you choose which apps Gemini can access, watch every step live, pause at any time, and approve key actions before they happen,” Michael Friedman, Google’s group product manager for the Gemini app, wrote in a blog post.

The Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently introduced AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability.

It has been revealed that google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The tech giant can also extend Gemini in other ways. Notably, it could bring Gemini’s computer use mode to additional operating systems and add features for business consumers. OpenAI’s Dots already includes capabilities designed to automate business workflows such as procurement.

Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.
  • Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules.
  • Industry observers note that the manufacturer confirmed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer confirmed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it notes can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson noted in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it stated already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson noted.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter stated.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

It has been revealed that the fresh complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

Sources indicate that on Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

Industry observers note that on Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

It has been revealed that compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the glitch in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the manufacturer’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS declared prepares for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Industry observers note that compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The manufacturer did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

In a recent development, below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.
